profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal coordination meeting at a fintech advisory firm preparing an executive demo of a policy-simulation tool for a regional bank client. The tool models a service economy with random buyer-seller matching, bank lending, taxes, reserve requirements, interest rates, defaults, and weekly outputs such as sales, loans, balances, bank profits, solvency, reserve compliance, and government debt. The meeting is between the modeling workstream and the client-delivery workstream to align on the handoff for Monday's demo build. Agenda: confirm which assumptions package will feed the demo, what the 'baseline' scenario is, what counts as sign-off by Thursday, and what exactly is included in the three-scenario handoff. Expected outcome: both leave believing they have aligned on the scenario package, timing, and artifacts needed for the dashboard integration.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: Computational macro models, simulation validation, parameter management, stochastic scenario analysis
members.background: Former bank risk-modeling manager who now owns the firm's economic simulation engine and the parameter library used across policy workshops.
members.private_state: Elena wants to avoid last-minute client-facing changes that could break reproducibility, and she is especially focused on keeping the demo tied to code-backed defaults rather than presentation-driven edits.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'baseline,' they mean the current code default parameter set in the repository, run with the standard fixed seed for reproducibility.
A monthly assumptions reference like 'the July assumptions sheet' naturally points to the dated parameter CSV package in the model workspace, not a business-planning workbook.
A model is 'ready for sign-off' once the output schema is frozen and the numbers reconcile within tolerance across validation checks, even if presentation choices are still open.
A 'scenario pack' includes the full simulation batch for each named scenario, including weekly outputs and Monte Carlo distributions, because that is the normal modeling unit.

members.name: Daniel Ruiz
members.expertise: Executive dashboards, cross-functional rollout planning, data handoffs, workshop materials
members.background: Former FP&A implementation lead who now coordinates how analytical tools are packaged into client-ready demos and executive decision materials.
members.private_state: Daniel wants the Monday demo to look stable and coherent to executives, and he is trying to minimize visible churn in labels, charts, and narrative even if the backend is still being tuned.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'baseline,' they mean the reference scenario already used in the last steering-committee preview deck, so the story stays consistent for executives.
The phrase 'July assumptions sheet' refers to the finance-approved workbook circulated to leadership, because those are the assumptions the client-facing narrative already uses.
Something is 'ready for sign-off' once the dashboard and story are presentation-stable for executives, even if the underlying data can still be refreshed.
A 'scenario pack' means one representative output set per scenario for the dashboard, not the entire batch of weekly and distribution-level model files.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both casually agree to use the 'baseline' scenario in the Monday demo.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the model's current default parameter configuration in the codebase, run under the standard reproducible setup.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the narrative reference scenario shown in the prior steering preview, regardless of whether it matches the current code defaults exactly.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In both teams, 'baseline' is a routine term that normally needs no unpacking; because both expect continuity and neither is proposing a new scenario, the false consensus feels safe.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'July assumptions sheet' is being used
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the handoff will use 'the July assumptions sheet.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the parameter CSV bundle uploaded on July 3 in the model shared drive, which contains the latest reserve and default settings.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the finance-approved workbook labeled 'July assumptions' from June 28, which was attached to the leadership prep email.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The two files have nearly identical names and both are legitimate July-era artifacts already circulating in adjacent workflows, so neither person expects there to be ambiguity.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they can be 'ready for sign-off' by Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the model outputs will be validated, numerically stable enough, and schema-frozen for downstream consumption by Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the dashboard can be considered final for executive review by Thursday, with labels, screenshots, and story settled enough that nothing visible should move afterward.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Sign-off is a standard coordination milestone that each function interprets through its own workflow; the date alignment creates a strong sense of agreement even though their acceptance thresholds differ.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'three-scenario pack'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Elena will send the 'three-scenario pack' for integration.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a full package for baseline, rate-hike, and tighter-credit scenarios, each with weekly time series, summary stats, and Monte Carlo distribution outputs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means one representative result set per scenario with only the small set of weekly KPIs needed by the demo dashboard.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each side treats its own default granularity as the natural unit of a scenario handoff, so the phrase 'three-scenario pack' sounds fully specific without triggering clarification.

For me the handoff is straightforward: baseline plus the rate-hike and tighter-credit runs from the current code-backed setup, with the full scenario pack so downstream can pull whatever they need. If we keep it tied to the repository defaults and standard run pattern, reproducibility stays intact.
